title: Mac (computer)
description: Family of personal computers made by Apple
wiki_lead:
Mac is a brand of personal computers designed and marketed by Apple since 1984. The name is short for Macintosh (its official name until 1999), a reference to the McIntosh apple. As of 2026, the product lineup includes the MacBook Neo, MacBook Air and MacBook Pro laptops, and the iMac, Mac Mini and Mac Studio desktops. Macs are currently sold with Apple's Unix-based macOS operating system, which is not licensed to other manufacturers and exclusively bundled with Mac computers. This operating system replaced Apple's original Macintosh operating system, which has variously been named System, Mac OS, and Classic Mac OS.
Jef Raskin conceived the Macintosh project in 1979, which was usurped and redefined by Apple co-founder Steve Jobs in 1981. The original Macintosh was launched in January 1984 at US$2,495 (equivalent to $7,700 in 2025), after Apple's "1984" advertisement during Super Bowl XVIII. A series of incrementally improved models followed, sharing the same integrated case design. In 1987, the Macintosh II brought color graphics, but was priced as a professional workstation and not a personal computer. Beginning in 1994 with the Power Macintosh, the Mac transitioned from Motorola 68000 series processors to PowerPC. Macintosh clones by other manufacturers were also briefly sold afterward. The line was refreshed in 1998 with the launch of the iMac G3, reinvigorating the line's competitiveness against commodity IBM PC compatibles. Macs transitioned to Intel x86 processors by 2006 along with new sub-product lines MacBook and Mac Pro. Since 2020, Macs have transitioned to Apple silicon chips based on ARM64.

History


1979–1984: Development

In the late 1970s, the Apple II became one of the most popular computers, especially in education. After IBM introduced the IBM PC in 1981, its sales surpassed the Apple II. In response, Apple introduced the Lisa in 1983. The Lisa's graphical user interface was inspired by strategically licensed demonstrations of the Xerox Star. Lisa surpassed the Star with intuitive direct manipulation, including the ability to drag and drop files, double-click to launch applications, and move or resize windows by clicking and dragging instead of going through a menu. However, hampered by its high price of $9,995 (equivalent to $35,000 in 2025) and lack of available software, the Lisa was commercially unsuccessful.
Parallel to the Lisa's development, a skunkworks team at Apple was working on the Macintosh project. Conceived in 1979 by Jef Raskin, Macintosh was envisioned as an affordable, easy-to-use computer for the masses. Raskin named the computer after his favorite type of apple, the McIntosh. The initial team consisted of Raskin, hardware engineer Burrell Smith, and Apple co-founder Steve Wozniak. In 1981, Steve Jobs was removed from the Lisa team and joined the Macintosh team. grok_lead: The Mac, short for Macintosh, is a family of personal computers designed, manufactured, and sold by Apple Inc. since its debut in 1984, renowned for introducing a graphical user interface (GUI), mouse-based navigation, and an all-in-one compact design that democratized personal computing for non-technical users. The original Macintosh 128K, priced at $2,495, featured 128 KB of RAM, a 9-inch monochrome display, and built-in applications like MacWrite and MacPaint, drawing inspiration from the Xerox Alto's interface but made affordable and mass-producible. Launched on January 24, 1984, following Apple's iconic "1984" Super Bowl commercial directed by Ridley Scott, it symbolized rebellion against conformist computing and quickly became a cultural icon despite initial sales challenges due to its limited expandability. The name "Macintosh" originated from the McIntosh apple variety, selected by project leader Jef Raskin as a nod to Apple's fruit-themed branding, with the spelling adjusted to avoid trademark conflicts with the audio company McIntosh Laboratory. Over four decades, the Mac has evolved through distinct eras, starting with Motorola 68000-based models in the 1980s that emphasized user-friendliness and creative tools, followed by PowerPC processors in the 1990s for enhanced performance in professional applications like desktop publishing and video editing. The transition to Intel processors in 2006 marked a pivotal shift, enabling broader software compatibility via Boot Camp, while the 2020 introduction of Apple silicon âcustom ARM-based chips like the M1âdelivered superior efficiency, battery life, and integration with iOS apps, powering modern features such as Apple Intelligence for AI tasks. Key milestones include the 1987 Macintosh II, Apple's first color and expandable desktop; the 1998 iMac G3, a translucent all-in-one that revived Apple's fortunes with internet-focused design; and the 2006 MacBook Pro, establishing the premium laptop standard. Today, the Mac lineup encompasses versatile laptops ( MacBook Air and MacBook Pro) for portability and professional workflows, and desktops ( iMac, Mac mini, Mac Studio, and Mac Pro) for creative and computational intensity, all running macOS âan operating system emphasizing security, ecosystem continuity with iPhone and iPad, and tools for developers, artists, and educators. With a loyal user base in industries like film, music, and software development, the Mac remains a benchmark for innovation, blending hardware-software synergy with privacy-focused design.
